adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.schema.ts:5 — no .max() on `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` + no rate limit on `addGuests: authedProcedure` (_router.tsx:79). Self-signup user self-books, then POSTs thousands of addresses; each gets a DKIM-signed, from-spoofed ICS with method:"REQUEST"/status:"CONFIRMED" that auto-inserts into victims' calendars. Phishing/calendar-spam amplifier. [P1, conf85]

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new authenticated `addGuests` mutation whose input schema is `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no upper bound (`.max(...)`) and no other throttling/quotas in the router. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the handler will `createMany` attendees for all provided emails (minus existing/blacklisted) and then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, which sends an email (with an ICS invite `method: "REQUEST"`, `status: "CONFIRMED"`) to every attendee in `calendarEvent.attendees` (i.e., including the newly added addresses). That makes it possible for any authorized user on a booking (including the organizer/attendee, which a self-signup user can be) to submit very large arrays and trigger mass outbound calendar-invite emails. While the exact DKIM/spoofing and victim auto-insert behavior depends on mail/calendar clients and infra not shown, the core amplifier vector (unbounded list -> mass email + ICS invites, no per-request cap/rate limit) is directly supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:52,149-156 — `const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(...)` grants add-guest power to any attendee; each new guest becomes an attendee and inherits it. Emails carry `booking.uid` + `evt.videoCallData = {..., password: videoCallReference?.meetingPassword, url: ...}`, so one attendee pushes join URL+password and cancel/reschedule links to arbitrary addresses. No organizer authorization, no removal path. [P2, conf80]

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, authorization explicitly allows any attendee to add guests: `const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);` and the guard is `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN;`, so being an attendee is sufficient. The handler then (1) persists new attendee emails via `attendees.createMany`, (2) builds a `CalendarEvent` containing `uid: booking.uid` and, if present, `evt.videoCallData` including `meetingPassword` and `meetingUrl`, and (3) sends emails to the full attendee list via `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, where new guests get `AttendeeScheduledEmail(...)`. This is a verifiable privilege/abuse vector introduced by the diff: an authenticated attendee can push meeting/join details (and any links embedded in the scheduled email template) to arbitrary addresses without organizer approval. The “inheritance” part is partially true (they become attendees), though new guests would only be able to call the endpoint themselves if they can authenticate as that email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/security][lens/feasibility] addGuests.handler.ts:158-163 — `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` builds EventManager from the CALLER's credentials, then `updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs them against the ORGANIZER's `booking.references`. Confused deputy; for any non-organizer caller the calendar silently never updates while the DB does. [P1, conf75-80]

adjudication.rationale: The handler explicitly allows non-organizers to add guests (`isAttendee` grants access). But when updating the external calendar it does `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user); const eventManager = new EventManager({ ...user, credentials }); await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);` where `user`/`ctx.user` is the caller, not the booking organizer. The diff even loads `booking.user.credentials` but never uses them. This makes the calendar update depend on the caller’s integrations/permissions, so an attendee (or other permitted non-organizer) can successfully update the DB attendees while the organizer’s calendar update is likely to fail/do nothing due to missing/wrong credentials (confused-deputy/correctness issue).

Team admins are denied; branch is dead if isTeamAdmin already covers OWNER. Also `teamId ?? 0` fires two membership queries against fictional team id 0 on every personal booking. [P1, conf80-100]

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/completeness][lens/data-migration] addGuests.handler.ts:92-171 — `prisma.booking.update` commits, then unguarded `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` at :165 (no try/catch, unlike the email call below). Provider 5xx → 500 to client, rows already committed, no emails sent; retry hits `if (uniqueGuests.length === 0) throw ... "emails_must_be_unique_valid"` (:80). Guest permanently in DB, never on calendar, never emailed, unaddable via UI. No transaction, no compensation, no idempotency key. [P1, conf75-85]

adjudication.rationale: The handler writes new attendees to the DB via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and only afterwards calls `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);` without any try/catch or transaction. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws (e.g., calendar provider failure), the mutation will reject/500 to the client after the DB commit. On retry, `uniqueGuests` is computed from the *pre-update* `booking.attendees` (from `findFirst`), but the next invocation will load the booking again and now those guests exist, making `uniqueGuests.length === 0` and throwing `BAD_REQUEST` (`emails_must_be_unique_valid`). This creates a verifiable partial-write failure mode: guests persist in DB but calendar update and subsequent email sending (which occurs later) may not happen, and the UI cannot re-add them to trigger the side effects.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/security][lens/completeness][lens/data-migration] addGuests.handler.ts:26-44 — `where: { id: bookingId }` with no `status`/`endTime` predicate. Guests addable to CANCELLED/REJECTED/past bookings; emails then ship `status:"CONFIRMED"`, `method:"REQUEST"` ICS (attendee-add-guests-email.ts:14-16), resurrecting a dead meeting on every calendar. adjudication.rationale: The new `addGuestsHandler` fetches the booking with `prisma.booking.findFirst({ where: { id: bookingId } ... })` and performs no check on booking state (e.g., CANCELLED/REJECTED) or time (past `endTime`). It then updates attendees and calls `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`. The new email templates explicitly generate an ICS with `status: "CONFIRMED"` and `method: "REQUEST"` (e.g., `packages/emails/templates/attendee-add-guests-email.ts`), which can re-invite attendees even if the original meeting was cancelled. This lack of status/time gating is a concrete correctness issue introduced by the diff; the UI reachability claim is not needed to validate the backend problem.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/security][lens/data-migration][lens/completeness] addGuests.handler.ts:70-78 — blacklist lowercased at :71, candidate never normalized: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. `Blocked@Example.com` bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entirely. matched_golden_ids: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same core flaw: the blacklist is normalized to lowercase but the incoming guest email is not, so `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` can be bypassed with uppercase/mixed-case emails. It even gives an example (`Blocked@Example.com`) consistent with the golden issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/architecture][lens/scope][lens/intent][lens/testing][lens/completeness] addGuests.handler.ts:168 — `await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the RAW input, not `uniqueGuests`. email-manager.ts:541 `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` then sends a pre-existing attendee a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` re-confirmation + fresh ICS REQUEST instead of the add-guests notice. [P1, conf85-100]

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the handler computes `uniqueGuests` by filtering out emails already in `booking.attendees` (and blacklisted), and uses `uniqueGuests` to create new attendee records. However, it later calls `await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` using the raw `guests` input, not `uniqueGuests`. In `email-manager.ts` `sendAddGuestsEmails(calEvent, newGuests)`, it checks `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` to decide to send `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (full reconfirmation + ICS REQUEST) vs `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. If the raw input includes an email of an existing attendee (e.g., user adds a mix of new + already-present emails), that existing attendee will be incorrectly treated as “new” and receive the scheduled/reconfirmation email again. This behavior is directly verifiable from the diff and is a correctness defect introduced by passing `guests` instead of `uniqueGuests`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/data-migration] addGuests.handler.ts:58-68 — `where: { id: booking.userId || 0 }` on findFirstOrThrow. `Booking.userId` is Int?; no user id 0 exists, so dynamic-group/unassigned bookings hard-fail with Prisma P2025 as a raw 500. Also redundant: booking already loaded at :35 with `user: { include: { credentials: true } }` — every encrypted credential row pulled and never read. [P1, conf85-90]

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the organizer lookup is `prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: booking.userId || 0 } ... })`. The use of `|| 0` indicates `booking.userId` can be null/undefined; in that case the query will search for id=0 and `findFirstOrThrow` will throw (Prisma P2025), which is not handled and will bubble as an internal error rather than a controlled TRPCError. Also, the initial booking fetch includes `user: { include: { destinationCalendar: true, credentials: true } }`, but this handler never reads `booking.user.credentials` (only potentially `booking.user.destinationCalendar`), so including `credentials` is unnecessary and causes extra sensitive/large data to be loaded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/completeness][lens/security][lens/data-migration][lens/scope] addGuests.handler.ts:83-106 — seated bookings unhandled: bare Attendee rows created with no BookingSeat, no `seatsPerTimeSlot` cap check — yet :145-146 copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` into evt, proving the author knew seated events reach here. In the diff, `evt` is constructed with `seatsPerTimeSlot` / `seatsShowAttendees` copied from `booking.eventType` (lines ~145-146), yet there is no check anywhere that `existingAttendees + uniqueGuests <= seatsPerTimeSlot` (or any similar cap enforcement) before writing to the DB or updating calendars. adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/completeness] addGuests.handler.ts:124-147 — hand-rolled `evt` instead of the shared cal-event builder: no `iCalUID`, no `iCalSequence`, no `team`, no `metadata`, no `bookerUrl`/`responses`. [lens/testing][lens/completeness] addGuests.handler.ts:167-171 — `catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` binds and discards `err`, no logger, still returns `{ message: "Guests added" }`. email-manager.ts:549 `Promise.all` means one bad recipient rejects the whole batch — no per-recipient isolation, no timeout, no retry, no diagnosable trace. adjudication.rationale: Yes. In addGuests.handler.ts the code wraps `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` in a `try/catch (err)` and then only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` without logging/using `err`, and regardless of failure it proceeds to `return { message: "Guests added" }`. Separately, in email-manager.ts `sendAddGuestsEmails` builds an array of email promises and `await Promise.all(emailsToSend);`, so a single `sendEmail` rejection will reject the whole `sendAddGuestsEmails` call (no per-email error handling inside that function). adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/testing][lens/architecture] AddGuestsDialog.tsx:26 — two different schemas share the name `ZAddGuestsInputSchema`: client is `z.array(...).refine(uniqueEmails.size === emails.length)` declared inside the render body (rebuilt every render); server (addGuests.schema.ts:5) is `z.object({bookingId, guests})` with no uniqueness refine and no `.min(1)`. Uniqueness is client-only; any non-browser tRPC caller bypasses it. [P2, conf85-100]

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:44 vs :55 — `NOT_FOUND booking_not_found` thrown BEFORE the permission check, on an unscoped sequential int id. Logged-in user walks bookingId 1..N and distinguishes FORBIDDEN (exists, not yours) from NOT_FOUND — cross-tenant enumeration oracle. `bookingsProcedure` (used by editLocation, _router.tsx:62) avoids this by scoping the query. Only after a booking is found does it compute `isTeamAdminOrOwner` / `isOrganizer` / `isAttendee` and potentially throw `FORBIDDEN`. This creates a distinguishable response pattern for an authenticated caller probing sequential integer `bookingId`s: nonexistent IDs yield NOT_FOUND, while existing-but-unauthorized bookings yield FORBIDDEN. adjudication_records.issue_text: [lens/intent][lens/scope][lens/testing] AddGuestsDialog.tsx:43-44 — `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`; showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error");` — a template literal is always truthy, so the new key `unable_to_add_guests` is unreachable dead code, and the toast renders literal `undefined: ...` when err.data is absent. [P3, conf95-100]

adjudication.rationale: In `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` the error handler builds `message` using a template literal: ```${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}```. Template literals always produce a string, so `message` is always truthy even when `err.data?.code` is `undefined` (yielding e.g. `"undefined: ..."`). Therefore `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` will never hit the fallback, making the new `unable_to_add_guests` toast text effectively unreachable and potentially displaying `undefined:` to users when `err.data` is absent.
